description: DataSquad is a team passionate about software, game development, and space exploration. We aim to create an interactive and educational experience where young learners can explore the challenges of managing a lunar or Martian mission.  We welcome teammates with skills in coding, game/web development, UI/UX and AI. Join us to build a creative and engaging prototype together.
summary:
Mars Outpost is a browser game in which kids run a Mars base for seven days. Players command two astronauts and make one decision per sol: make air, make water, grow food, retrieve a rock, call Earth, or spend a day hiding from a solar storm. Power, water, air and food drain daily, and every job card shows the cost and the remaining supplies before the player commits. There is no safe option; even resting burns a day.

The game addresses the challenge by turning a mission's real trade-offs into play rather than explanation. Radiation shielding costs a full day of production. Communication delay means Earth cannot answer in time. Supplies must be produced, never received. The terrain comes from NASA's Valles Marineris model, oxygen figures from the Perseverance MOXIE experiment, and the communication delay from real Mars data — all cited inside the game.

It matters because it gives 7–12 year olds a decision-making instinct about deep-space survival in ten browser-playable minutes, with no download and no account.
details:
Mars Outpost

Seven days. Two astronauts. One rock.

Purpose

  • Space content for kids usually shows the answer — a poster, a fact, a rocket. It rarely shows the decision behind it.
  • We built a game where the decision is the content: seven days, one job a day, no free choices.
  • Purpose: let a 7–12 year old feel what mission planners actually weigh — power, air, food, radiation — in ten minutes.

What it does

  • Two astronauts, one base, seven days, one Mars rock to bring home.
  • Each day you do one job: make air, make water, pick food, get the rock, call Earth, save power, hide from a storm, or rest.
  • Power, water, air and food drain daily. Anything that hits zero hurts the crew.
  • Every job card shows the cost and what you'll have left at the end of the day — before you commit.
  • Day 4 opens the rock site, and it is the only day Earth can answer you. Day 5 is a solar storm: hide, or lose 25 health each.
  • Best ending: both astronauts home at full health, rock on board. Worst: medical evacuation.

What you learn

  • The base has to make everything itself. Water, air and food run out every single day.
  • The Sun doesn't always help. Dust blocks the light and halves your power.
  • You can't block radiation — only hide from it. Mars has no magnetic field; the bunker is the only shield.
  • Earth is too far. A message takes 3 to 22 minutes one way, so sometimes you must decide alone.
  • Every shortcut is paid back. Power saved today returns tomorrow as lost air or lost health.
  • People get tired. Two days in a row costs extra power; someone has to rest.

Benefits

  • Kids feel a trade-off instead of reading about one.
  • Failure is cheap: ten minutes a run, instant restart, try a different plan.
  • The science is traceable: NASA's Valles Marineris terrain, MOXIE oxygen figures, real Mars communication delay — sources open inside the game.

Intended impact

  • For ages 7–12 and classrooms: one run fits inside a lesson, no download, no account.
  • Kids leave understanding that deep-space missions are decided by resource trade-offs, not luck.

Tools used

  • Godot 4.7.2 with GDScript, exported to the browser and hosted on Vercel.
  • NASA 3D terrain model, CC0 audio and textures, original UI drawn in-engine.

How it's creative

  • The trade-off is the game, not a theme painted on top.
  • Radiation is a choice, not a meter — the only shield is a day of hiding.
  • Communication delay becomes gameplay: you cannot wait for Earth's answer, so you must decide.

Factors we considered

  • Age 7–12: one decision per day, plain words, no jargon.
  • Challenge guidance: four resources plus health — not six systems to track.
  • Access: runs in a browser, works with touch and mouse, offers performance presets.
  • Honesty: game numbers are labelled as game numbers; real NASA figures are cited.
